title: How to keep lights on during long still, dark spells: storage, scale and policy
label: 21 October 2026 · Dunkelflaute and intermittency
summary: Witnesses from the Faraday Institution and the Energy Storage Association told peers that the UK needs a wide portfolio of long-duration storage—mechanical, thermal and novel batteries—to manage rare but severe low-wind, low-sun 'Dunkelflaute' events and to harvest otherwise-curtailed renewable energy. Some technologies are market-ready but small today; others (iron- and aluminium-based long-duration batteries) could be cheap enough to compete with unabated gas but need 5–10 years of development and supportive policy, market signals and payments to investors.

glossary.definition: A weather period with very low wind and solar output, causing low renewable electricity generation.
When renewables are producing more energy than can be used, so operators are paid or told not to generate.
When generation exists but can't reach demand because transmission lines are full or constrained.
A government support model offering revenue floors and caps to make long-duration storage projects bankable.
A contract giving renewable generators a fixed price, insulating them from market price swings.
Two reservoirs at different heights; water is pumped up to store energy and released to generate electricity.
Energy stored by compressing air in tanks or underground caverns then expanded to generate power.
Energy stored by cooling air into a liquid and re-gasifying it to drive a turbine.
A battery chemistry using iron and oxygen in an aqueous system suited to very low-cost, long-duration storage.
An aluminium-based battery chemistry using water-based electrolytes, aimed at very low cost per kWh.
A metal used in vanadium redox flow batteries, better for medium-duration storage but costly and low energy density.
An underground hollow in salt deposits used to store gases or compressed air at large scale.
A UK grant programme (Long Duration Energy Storage) to support early-stage, higher-risk storage technologies.

chapters.title: Why long-duration storage matters
chapters.takeaway: Storage can both replace some gas-fired backup and capture otherwise-wasted renewable energy, reducing import dependence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are examining Dunkelflaute and whether we need long-duration storage as part of the clean power plan to 2030. Please introduce yourselves.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: I'm a senior policy consultant at the Energy Storage Association; we represent firms working on long-duration storage and advise on policy and market access.

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: I'm Special Projects Director at the Faraday Institution, which funds battery research and early-stage commercialisation in the UK.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What's the added value of long-duration storage—pumped hydro, compressed air, ultra-long batteries—compared with low-carbon dispatchable power?

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: First, energy security: the UK risks rising import dependence for fossil fuels by the mid-2030s. Second, storage can harvest curtailed renewables rather than letting them go unused.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: System operator forecasts show around 29–30 TWh/year of unabated gas output mid-2030s, while 'economic curtailment' could reach ~50 TWh and congestion curtailment may add similarly.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: So, up to ~100 TWh of potential clean energy could be lost without storage. Long-duration storage can shift those electrons to when they're needed.

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: Batteries of 100+ hours could help. Our modelling shows 3 TWh of ultra-long storage could absorb a lot of surplus energy and cut reliance on gas.

chapters.title: Which technologies and when?
chapters.takeaway: Some options are ready in modest scale today; novel aqueous aluminium and iron-air batteries could be very cheap but need 5–10 years to scale.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: Is this a question of scaling current lithium tech or do we need new chemistries to reach the terawatt-hour scale?

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: Lithium-ion and sodium-ion can't reach the low installed costs we need for ultra-long-duration cycling—they're optimised for frequent cycling and vehicles.

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: Targets for ultra-long batteries are around £11–£15 per kWh installed. We think aqueous aluminium and iron-air could hit that because they're simpler to manufacture.

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: Timeline: 5–7 years of research to large MWh demonstrators, then 2–3 years to scale to GWh projects—so availability in the second half of the 2030s; terawatt-hour scale by 2050 is plausible.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Meanwhile, there are practical alternatives now: flow batteries (vanadium and other chemistries), zinc-based systems and mechanical storage. They won't be ultra-long, but they help early in an event.

turns.speaker: Lord Lennie
turns.text: Rough cost comparison?

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: Our target for aqueous aluminium/iron-air is £11–£15/kWh installed. Vanadium flow batteries are well north of £100/kWh installed and have low energy density.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Energy density matters because it affects site size and cost. Some technologies can go underground—compressed air in caverns—others are surface-based.

chapters.title: Compressed air, liquid air, pumped hydro and land use
chapters.takeaway: Compressed and liquid air are proven and can scale but are small in the UK now; pumped hydro is mature but geographically constrained; land can be managed by reusing brownfield and retiring gas sites.

turns.speaker: Baroness Coffey
turns.text: What's the likely contribution from compressed-air and liquid-air by 2030 and 2040?

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Both are proven. The UK has small projects now: one compressed-air project won a cap and floor 'window 1' place (15 MW, 30‑hour duration). Highview's liquid-air plant at Carrington is nearing commercial scale.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: By 2030 they'll be a fraction of total storage. By 2040 their share depends heavily on policy and project pipeline; internationally China is already building many such projects.

turns.speaker: Baroness Coffey
turns.text: Where are the salt caverns for compressed air?

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: They're concentrated in Yorkshire, Cheshire and Dorset, and some shallow offshore options exist. Caverns are a strategic storage asset that could host gas, biomethane, hydrogen or compressed air.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How do compressed air and hydrogen compare on energy density and round-trip efficiency?

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Natural gas is 4–5× more energy dense than hydrogen. Compressed air is ~10–15× less energy-dense than the same hydrogen amount. Round-trip efficiency: hydrogen is in the high 30s percent today, compressed air mid-60s.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: What about pumped hydro and pumped thermal—space and schedule?

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: The UK has not built pumped hydro for 40 years but several projects are in cap and floor window 1. Lead time from final investment to commissioning is 5–10 years; two projects aim for 2030–33. Pumped thermal is earlier stage in the UK.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: People worry about batteries in the countryside and safety. Where should we site these?

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: Ultra-long aqueous aluminium and iron-air batteries are expected to be much safer than lithium-ion and are suited to sites near where offshore wind lands or where gas plants are retiring—reusing existing grid connections.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: But pumped hydro has environmental impacts in scenic areas—how do we balance that?

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: We need everything. Pumped hydro will be part of an overall mix; planning must balance environmental costs with the need for reliable, low-carbon power.

chapters.title: Policy, markets and what needs to change
chapters.takeaway: The UK needs clearer central demand signals, support payments for security-focused assets, incentives for technology diversity, and better alignment across CfD, transmission planning and the capacity market.

turns.speaker: Lord Lennie
turns.text: If you were Secretary of State, what policy gaps would you fix first?

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: For ultra-long batteries: they will likely be used for system security, not to chase maximum merchant revenue. That means system-operator control and government-backed payments to remove investor risk—similar to arrangements for nuclear or reserved capacity.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: We'd want a centralised, authoritative view of demand for long-duration storage so developers and investors know what's needed. Right now everyone is estimating for themselves.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Second, encourage technology diversity. The current focus on pumped hydro and lithium in cap and floor window 1 risks crowding out other options before they mature.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Third, fund another LoDES-style round to bridge demonstrators to commercial scale; that gap is often tens of millions and prevents promising projects from progressing.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Fourth, better join CfD auctions, transmission planning and the capacity market so storage is planned alongside generation rather than left to mop up curtailment after the fact.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: Could CfDs be evolved to require some shaping or firming by generators?

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Yes—over time CfDs could ratchet in shaping obligations so generators help manage intermittency at source, reducing downstream balancing needs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final sharp points?

turns.speaker: Nick Smailes
turns.text: Technology-wise we can get low-cost long-duration batteries, but only with sustained R&D, demonstration, and payment models that reward security rather than pure market returns.

turns.speaker: Andy McNeill
turns.text: Practically: use brownfield and retiring gas sites, don't pick winners too early, and create clearer demand and revenue routes so a mix of compressed air, liquid air, pumped hydro, flow batteries and novel chemistries can scale.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both; we appreciate the practical timelines and the clear policy asks. We'll move to the next panel.
